title: On Worst-Case Guarantees for Graph-Based Nearest-Neighbor Search
claim: Placing auxiliary points along a random projection lets a greedy graph walk reproduce a hashing bucket lookup.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, projection on left, resulting directed graph on right
description: The left panel shows a 2-D point cloud of labeled data points x1 to x12, colored in five groups (red, blue, orange, teal, magenta). Dotted gray lines project each point onto a diagonal arrowed line labeled v. Short double-arc tick marks split the line into five buckets. Inside each bucket is a colored star Steiner point, s1 to s5, in the matching color. A black star s0 sits off the line, away from the data. The right panel is a directed graph. s0 sends arrows to s1 through s5, and each colored Steiner point sends arrows to the data points of its own color. Colors link the two panels. The eye goes first to the colored stars and the projection lines.
caption: We illustrate the basic building block of our graph-based simulation of the projection-based LSH method of [ref]. Steiner points $s_1, \ldots, s_5$ are placed along a random line, $v$, and one additional Steiner point, $s_0$, is placed far away from the dataset. Running greedy search on the directed search graph on the right, starting at $s_0$, implements the core LSH primitive: for a query $q$, it will first search for nearest neighbors among all points that project into the same bucket on $v$.
abstract: Graph-based nearest neighbor search algorithms like HNSW, DiskANN, NSG, and others have surged in popularity in recent years due to their excellent empirical performance in comparison to space-partitioning methods like IVF data structures and Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH). However, in contrast to LSH and related methods, obtaining strong worst-case theoretical guarantees for graph-based search has proven challenging. In this paper, we prove a strong lower bound that helps explain the lack of progress towards such guarantees. We show that no standard graph-based method (any that runs a variant of greedy search on a flat or hierarchical graph) can achieve sublinear query time for approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space, even for an arbitrarily large approximation factor. On the other hand, we prove that sublinear query time is possible if we allow for Steiner points in the search graph. We obtain bounds comparable to LSH, showing e.g., that graph-based search with Steiner points can solve $c$-approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space with query time $\tilde{O}(n^{1/(c-1)})$. We complement this result with initial experiments exploring how Steiner points can be incorporated into practical graph-based methods.
